description:
We are Computer Science students at FCFM (UANL). We have solid experience in software development and data analysis, with a strong interest in integrating Artificial Intelligence and Machine Learning models into real, functional applications.

We are a focused team, but above all, we love collaborating and learning new things.
summary: Cropro helps Mexican farmers make better crop rotation decisions. For any location in Mexico it brings together NASA Earth observations (SMAP, MODIS, GRACE, SRTM, POWER) with local soil, crop requirements, pest risk and market prices, and turns them into clear charts, alerts and a suggestion of what to plant next, always with the reason behind it. It supports the farmer's judgment; it does not replace it.
details:
The problem. Farmers in Mexico face shifting temperatures, irregular rainfall, water scarcity and declining soil health, but the data to plan around them is scattered across NASA, government and market sources that are hard to read and rarely local. Cropro puts it in one place, for the farmer’s own location.

What it does.

  • Climate and soil dashboard. Daily conditions for the active location (temperature, rain, wind, soil moisture and temperature, a “good window for field work” indicator) and a map of Mexico with rain and heat layers.
  • Soil health. pH, organic carbon and texture (SoilGrids), measured soil moisture and drought status (SMAP), vegetation and bare-soil periods (MODIS), terrain slope (SRTM) and regional water-storage trend (GRACE).
  • Rotation suggestions. For each plot, the next crop is chosen to restore or use soil nitrogen (legume ↔ cereal) and to avoid the same botanical family, which breaks pest and disease cycles. Candidates come from a catalog of 399 crops, and every suggestion shows its reason.
  • Planting window. Crop temperature requirements (FAO EcoCrop) checked against NASA POWER climate history, adjusted when the soil is drier than normal.
  • Alerts. Frost, heat, rain deficit or waterlogging per crop, dry soil, and pest risk from the EPPO pest database combined with local weather.
  • Market and economics. Producer price, yield and trend by state or municipality (SIAP), consumer price trend (Profeco), and cost and income per planting in the planner, with CSV and PDF export.
  • News. Agricultural and Earth-observation news (CIMMYT, NASA Earth Observatory).

How we use NASA data.

  • SMAP: soil moisture measured from space (9 km, since 2015). We use it for drought status because NASA POWER changed model on 1 Oct 2026 and comparing it with its own history gave false droughts.
  • MODIS: NDVI at 250 m (crop vigor and bare-soil periods) and land cover.
  • GRACE: regional water-storage trend.
  • SRTM: elevation and slope at 30 m.
  • NASA POWER: historical climate and root-zone soil moisture.

Who it is for. Less experienced farmers get plain-language suggestions with reasons; advanced users get the underlying charts and numbers.

Limitations (we say them in the app too).

  • SMAP, GRACE and POWER are coarse (km to hundreds of km). They show regional trends, not a single plot, and should be complemented with ground observations.
  • Pest-risk thresholds are still being calibrated; no open pest dataset exists for Mexico.
  • The effect of each rotation on pests and nutrients is curated knowledge (nitrogen fixation, botanical family), not measured data, and should be validated with an agronomist.
  • Only about 80 of the 399 crops have complete family and nitrogen data; the rest are inferred from crop type.

Next steps. Compare several complete rotation strategies side by side (including the farmer’s current one) with evidence, risks and information gaps; use water and price in the rotation score; add NASA GPM rainfall and a SMAP layer to the map.

Built with Python (FastAPI), React, Docker and GitHub.
